items.bodyEn: Sakashita, 'below the slope', was the last stop before the Suzuka Pass, the Tōkaidō's great western climb, paired with Hakone. A flood in 1650 destroyed the original town nearer the pass, and it was rebuilt a little downhill. Small as it was, it kept three honjin and some forty-eight inns for travelers resting before or after the climb.
items.sourceNote: 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843); Hiroshige, 'Sakanoshita: Fudesute-mine' (c. 1833)

items.titleEn: The Mountain That Beat a Painter
items.bodyEn: Across the gorge from Sakashita rises 筆捨山, Brush-Throwing Mountain. Tradition says the painter Kanō Motonobu set out to paint it, but its clouds and colors shifted so quickly that he gave up and threw away his brush, and the peak took the name. Hiroshige drew it in his Sakanoshita print: travelers at a teahouse gazing across at the crags.

items.titleEn: 三昧: From Meditation to Binge
items.bodyEn: The suffix 〜三昧, as in 読書三昧, a reading spree, or 贅沢三昧, a life of luxury, is Sanskrit. 三昧 transcribes samādhi, the deep absorption of Buddhist meditation. Being wholly absorbed in one thing slid from a monk's virtue to anyone's indulgence. Alone it is read さんまい; attached as a suffix it voices to ざんまい.
items.ja: {読書三昧|どくしょざんまい}
items.sourceNote: Kōjien (Iwanami), entry 三昧: 梵語 samādhi の音写; Daijisen

items.bodyEn: The ゆえ of this station's 〜ゆえに is written 故. The Shuowen Jiezi explains it as 'to make something happen', built from 攵, the striking hand, with 古, old, lending the sound. A cause makes things happen, so 故 means reason: ゆえに, therefore; 事故, an incident. 故 also shares 古's sense of old and former: 故郷, hometown; 故人, the departed.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 故: 使為之也, 从攴古聲; Kanjigen (Gakken)
